data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Preferring the better-corroborated theory is defensible on Popper's terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-inductive 'methodological rule' to maximize the severity of future tests; the cost of accepting this is the abandonment of the hope that science converges toward probable truth, leaving us with only a track record of error-elimination without assurance of predictive reliability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd/Miller proof renders verisimilitude formally undefinable, the link between corroboration and 'closeness to truth' collapses, making the preference arbitrary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory (e.g., building a bridge) inherently requires an inductive leap regarding future performance, then any justification for preference smuggles induction back in.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's distinction between 'logical probability' and 'degree of corroboration' cannot sustain a practical decision procedure without implicitly relying on the uniformity of nature.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The preference functions as a strategic heuristic: since high corroboration indicates a theory has survived severe tests (high empirical content/improbability), choosing it maximizes the potential information gain from the next test. If the theory fails, we learn more; if it survives, our confidence in its high content grows without assigning it higher probability. This avoids induction by treating the preference as a rule for generating knowledge (error elimination) rather than a prediction of utility.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
